loading-and-cleaning.advanced: The worker plans the order and layout for loading materials so machines keep running without creating safety hazards. For example, they arrange sheet metal carts beside a press to streamline feeding and keep aisles clear.
loading-and-cleaning.basic: The worker places raw materials into machine holders and wipes down work tables while an experienced operator supervises. For example, they slide steel sheets into a press tray and clean away oily metal scraps.

machine-setup-and-controls.advanced: The worker diagnoses and adjusts machine parameters when changing production jobs to keep cuts exact. For example, they adjust stamping pressure and blade depth when switching from thin aluminum to thick plastic sheets.

measuring-workpieces.advanced: The worker tests measuring gauges against known reference blocks and defines how parts must be measured on new products. For example, they calibrate digital calipers and write step-by-step sizing rules for a stamped automotive bracket.

operating-cutting-machines.advanced: The worker manages several running presses at once to keep work moving smoothly and ensure protective guards stay in place. For example, they patrol three cutting stations, checking production pace and emergency interlocks.
operating-cutting-machines.basic: The worker powers up machinery and watches it run while following instructions from an experienced coworker. For example, they press the cycle start button on a sheet metal punch and watch for jams.

reading-production-specs.advanced: The worker reviews multi-step job sheets and technical blueprints to catch conflicting measurements before cutting begins. For example, they notice that a specified hole location overlaps with a planned bend line and correct it.

adjusting-machine-settings.advanced: The worker tunes drill speeds and feeds for hard-to-cut metals and guides others on tool upkeep. For example, they adjust drill settings to bore titanium cleanly and show coworkers how to check drill bits for wear.
adjusting-machine-settings.basic: The worker swaps dull drill bits and turns fluid valves while an experienced colleague watches. For example, they loosen a chuck to put in a fresh drill bit and adjust the nozzle spraying cooling liquid.

laying-out-reference-points.advanced: The worker plans where to mark centerlines on complex workpieces and checks positions using sensitive dial gauges. For example, they map hole locations across an engine block and use a dial indicator to confirm exact centering.

measuring-workpiece-accuracy.advanced: The worker establishes rules for checking drilled holes and teaches coworkers how to measure delicate features. For example, they demonstrate how to use an internal bore gauge to measure cylinder diameters within hair-thin limits.

operating-drilling-machines.advanced: The worker resolves machine faults, moves heavy parts using safe lifting techniques, and sharpens dull drill bits. For example, they diagnose strange motor noises, use a crane to load a heavy gear, and regrind worn cutters.
operating-drilling-machines.basic: The worker brings the spinning drill down to the material and starts the automatic feed while supervised. For example, they guide the drill head to the surface of a metal plate and pull the power lever.

reading-machining-plans.advanced: The worker studies engineering diagrams to clarify unclear hole dimensions and guides newer staff through the plan. For example, they calculate an unlisted bore depth from overall part dimensions and explain the drawing to an apprentice.

setting-up-workpieces.advanced: The worker creates custom holding frames and clamps odd-shaped parts so they stay steady during drilling. For example, they build a specialized clamp to hold an angled plastic housing firmly in place.

equipment-monitoring-and-repair.advanced: The worker replaces broken mechanical assemblies and consults engineers when difficult machine breakdowns occur. For example, they disassemble a worn grinding spindle, replace damaged bearings, and review blueprint tolerances with an engineer.
equipment-monitoring-and-repair.basic: The worker watches and listens to running equipment to notice malfunctions with help from an experienced mentor. For example, they listen for abnormal grinding noises or watch for excessive vibration on a polishing belt.

machine-setup-and-controls.advanced: The worker fixes grinding machine configuration errors and advises other operators on the best operational settings. For example, they adjust wheel speed and table movement to stop parts from overheating and teach teammates the setup.

precision-measurement-and-inspection.advanced: The worker creates inspection rules for part smoothness and teaches colleagues how to handle delicate measuring devices. For example, they set allowable surface roughness limits and show staff how to use a precision micrometer.

tool-selection-and-lubrication.advanced: The worker chooses specialized abrasive wheels for demanding polishing jobs and directs how cooling fluid is applied. For example, they pick a diamond grinding wheel for hardened steel and adjust the fluid nozzle to prevent scorching.

workpiece-positioning-and-mounting.advanced: The worker creates secure clamping methods for oddly shaped parts and coaches new staff on safe mounting. For example, they design a custom magnetic holding block to grip a curved turbine blade during surface grinding.

blueprint-reading.advanced: The worker uses geometry and trigonometry to calculate cutting angles and rotation speeds directly from part diagrams. For example, they compute the exact taper angle needed to machine a conical metal pin on a lathe.

machine-upkeep.advanced: The worker writes and enters code into computerized machines so they shape parts automatically without human intervention. For example, they type coordinate commands into a computerized lathe to turn fifty identical brass fittings.

quality-inspection.advanced: The worker turns handwheels to move machine parts manually through a full cycle, checking clearances before running power. For example, they hand-crank a lathe carriage to ensure the cutting tool clears the chuck without colliding.

tool-maintenance.advanced: The worker chooses the right cutting blades based on metal hardness and mathematical calculations. For example, they calculate surface speed to pick a heat-resistant carbide cutting insert for turning stainless steel rods.

workpiece-setup.advanced: The worker mounts mechanical guides and rotating cam plates on a lathe to control how metal moves during turning. For example, they install shaped metal cams to guide a cutting tool along a tapered shaft.

blueprint-interpretation.advanced: The worker examines detailed technical drawings to decide which cutting tools to use and in what order. For example, they review a blueprint to plan rough milling passes before finishing intricate slots with a fine cutter.

cutting-operation.advanced: The worker oversees machines that carve metal from multiple directions simultaneously and fixes material movement problems. For example, they monitor a multi-direction mill shaping a curved propeller blade and resolve a stuttering table feed.

machine-parameter-setting.advanced: The worker sets cutting speeds and feed rates for uncommon alloys and teaches coworkers optimal techniques. For example, they adjust milling speeds to shape nickel metal cleanly and coach teammates on avoiding tool wear.

quality-verification.advanced: The worker sets dimensional tolerance benchmarks and verifies that milled components line up precisely before assembly. For example, they measure milled mating surfaces with an indicator gauge to verify alignment before parts are bolted together.

tool-maintenance.advanced: The worker creates upkeep schedules for machine cutters and teaches coworkers how to sharpen blades safely. For example, they set inspection intervals for milling bits and demonstrate safe wheel grinding techniques to apprentices.

workpiece-setup.advanced: The worker instructs coworkers on how to clamp tricky materials and install heavy cutting tools into milling machines. For example, they show an operator how to clamp an uneven casting squarely in a machine vise.

equipment-maintenance.basic: The worker cleans, lubricates, and performs basic maintenance on shop equipment so it operates smoothly. For example, they clear metal shavings from machine ways, wipe down surfaces, and pump fresh oil into lubrication points daily.

machine-setup.advanced: The worker invents and fabricates specialized clamps and cutting tools to build unique parts requested by engineers. For example, they build a custom aluminum fixture to hold an irregularly shaped aircraft bracket steady during machining.
machine-setup.basic: The worker bolts clamps and cutting tools onto shop machines and checks that they sit straight. For example, they mount a metal vise onto a milling table and tighten the bolts using a wrench.

precision-machining.advanced: The worker configures and runs specialized shaping machines to produce parts with extremely tight tolerances. For example, they set up a precision boring mill to cut bearing holes accurate to within one thousandth of an inch.

production-logging.advanced: The worker reviews smelting records over time to identify efficiency patterns and recommend ways to boost melt output. For example, they analyze temperature logs to reduce fuel consumption during overnight metal melting cycles.

furnace-control.advanced: The worker diagnoses furnace heating failures and establishes precise temperature targets for new metal mixtures. For example, they fix uneven burner flames and set exact melt temperatures for a newly introduced copper alloy.

ingot-transport.advanced: The worker plans factory travel routes for moving heavy cast metal blocks and trains forklift operators on workplace safety. For example, they map designated transport lanes and teach drivers how to haul heavy metal stacks safely.

metal-pouring.advanced: The worker adjusts how quickly molten metal enters intricate molds and mentors newer pourers on hand control. For example, they regulate ladle tilting speed to prevent air bubbles and teach assistants steady pouring technique.
metal-pouring.basic: The worker shovels or loads raw metal and purifying powder into a melting furnace while a supervisor watches. For example, they add scrap iron blocks and bags of chemical flux into a melting chamber.

mold-preparation.advanced: The worker defines cleanliness criteria for casting cavities and trains colleagues on how to inspect molds before pouring molten metal. For example, they teach workers how to check for loose sand particles using an inspection lamp.

scrap-management.advanced: The worker creates procedures to skim melting waste efficiently and reclaim leftover metal to reduce scrap. For example, they introduce a skimming tool to remove surface impurities without scooping out valuable liquid bronze.

assembly-and-tool-making.advanced: The worker designs and builds specialized holding frames and shaping molds for experimental prototypes. For example, they craft a silicone mold and alignment frame to cast test models of a new handheld device.

documentation-and-collaboration.advanced: The worker consults with design engineers to identify and resolve physical fit issues in prototype designs. For example, they meet with an engineering team to point out a fragile plastic clip and propose a thicker joint.

machine-setup-and-operation.advanced: The worker writes code for computer numerical control (CNC) machines to mill prototype components to precise sizes. For example, they input tool paths into a computerized router to carve a miniature plastic car bumper.

quality-inspection-and-rework.advanced: The worker sets measurement standards for experimental prototypes and coaches coworkers on conducting inspections. For example, they define allowable gaps between prototype plastic panels and show colleagues how to measure them with gauges.

blueprint-interpretation.advanced: The worker finds and reconciles contradictory measurements in blueprints and explains drawing conventions to junior patternmakers. For example, they resolve a conflict between overall length and section thickness, guiding an apprentice on reading the revision.

digital-modeling.advanced: The worker builds three-dimensional digital shapes on a computer and teaches colleagues how to use design software. For example, they model an intricate pattern for a pump housing and coach teammates on drafting tools.

machining-and-assembly.advanced: The worker writes computer numerical control programs to carve intricate pattern pieces and manages the restoration of damaged components. For example, they program a mill to cut replacement pattern sections and supervise bonding them into place.
machining-and-assembly.basic: The worker helps fit pattern parts together and cleans rough spots off surfaces using manual hand tools. For example, they hold pattern sections while a partner clamps them, then scrape excess glue with a file.

pattern-design.advanced: The worker designs molds that create hollow cavities inside metal castings and chooses durable materials for the job. For example, they engineer an aluminum box to press sand into internal shapes for engine parts.

precision-measurement.advanced: The worker defines accuracy benchmarks for casting patterns and tracks down why dimensions do not match the design. For example, they set shrinkage allowance rules and investigate why a finished plastic pattern is slightly oversized.

core-assembly-and-reinforcement.advanced: The worker plans internal rod frameworks to keep large sand cores from breaking under hot metal pressure. For example, they arrange metal support wires inside a fragile sand core before baking and assembling it.
core-assembly-and-reinforcement.basic: The worker packs and shapes sand blocks around pattern forms using manual tools. For example, they press damp sand into a wooden frame with a hand rammer and scrape the top flat with a straightedge.

mold-channel-cutting.advanced: The worker calculates and carves channels into sand molds so molten metal flows smoothly into every cavity. For example, they widen a pouring channel and carve feeder gates to prevent air pockets in a thin-walled casting.

mold-parting-and-removal.advanced: The worker selects specialized release sprays or powders so deep or intricate patterns pull out of sand cleanly. For example, they pick a liquid release coating for a ribbed pattern to prevent sand edges from crumbling.
mold-parting-and-removal.basic: The worker dusts non-stick powder over patterns under supervision so sand releases cleanly without sticking. For example, they shake a powder bag over a metal pattern to coat it before packing sand into the mold.

mold-surface-finishing.advanced: The worker sets surface smoothness rules for sand molds and defines how damaged cavities must be repaired. For example, they create inspection criteria for mold walls and instruct the crew on patching chips with mold paste.
mold-surface-finishing.basic: The worker smooths sand mold walls and cleans out shaping boxes with guidance from an experienced molder. For example, they brush away loose sand and use a small hand trowel to patch minor dents.

pattern-placement-and-clamping.advanced: The worker coaches coworkers on lining up multi-piece patterns accurately inside casting frames so mold halves match. For example, they show teammates how to use guide pins to align a two-piece valve pattern before packing sand.
pattern-placement-and-clamping.basic: The worker sets shaping patterns into mold frames and secures them under the supervision of a lead worker. For example, they center a wooden gear pattern inside a metal mold box and tighten the side clamps.

sand-packing-and-ramming.advanced: The worker inspects how tightly foundry sand is packed into mold boxes to stop molten metal from leaking or trapping gas. For example, they adjust pneumatic packing tools to eliminate soft pockets around a mold pattern.

equipment-handling.advanced: The worker diagnoses loose hydraulic, water, or electrical connections and directs the safe teardown of heavy molding machinery. For example, they fix a leaking cooling line coupler and instruct coworkers on safely unbolting a die press.

machine-setup.advanced: The worker fine-tunes temperature, pressure, and timing settings on molding equipment and trains coworkers on setup steps. For example, they adjust injection pressure for a multi-piece plastic part and walk a new operator through the controls.

mold-maintenance.advanced: The worker builds routine cleaning schedules for production molds and teaches workers proper upkeep procedures. For example, they set inspection intervals for metal mold cavities and show staff how to clean venting holes safely.

process-monitoring.advanced: The worker tracks machine sensor data and cycle times to stop parts from jamming and boost overall output. For example, they detect temperature spikes causing plastic parts to stick and adjust coolant flow to keep cycles smooth.

quality-inspection.advanced: The worker establishes quality criteria for molded parts and guides the crew in fixing repeat manufacturing flaws. For example, they identify recurring warping on plastic housings and instruct operators to lengthen the cooling cycle time.

reading-work-orders.advanced: The worker studies detailed blueprints to map out molding stages and clarify conflicting drawing details before manufacturing. For example, they review part thickness callouts to plan cooling times and resolve a mismatch between two blueprint views.

equipment-maintenance.advanced: The worker handles routine mechanical and electrical repairs and identifies when equipment requires specialized industrial service. For example, they replace a worn drive belt or faulty power switch and flag a damaged main motor for overhaul.

machine-operation.advanced: The worker monitors several running machines at once and quickly frees stuck parts to keep production moving. For example, they run a lathe and drill press concurrently, safely dislodging a jammed metal rod without long delays.
machine-operation.basic: The worker starts machine tools and turns on coolant pumps and automatic feed levers under direct supervision. For example, they push the motor start button, open the coolant valve, and engage the table feed handle.

machine-setup.advanced: The worker walks teammates through intricate tooling setups and operating steps across different shop machinery. For example, they guide an operator through setting stop limits on a lathe before transferring parts to a milling station.
machine-setup.basic: The worker mounts and clamps workpieces into machine holding devices with guidance from a senior operator. For example, they place a round metal bar into a three-jaw chuck and tighten it using a chuck wrench.

quality-inspection.advanced: The worker uses mathematical formulas to calculate gear tooth profiles and machine dial settings. For example, they compute gear pitch and tooth depth using shop math to set index plates for cutting gear teeth.
quality-inspection.basic: The worker checks finished pieces for visible flaws and size errors using metal rulers and shaping templates under guidance. For example, they overlay a curved template onto a cut metal plate to verify edge contours.

technical-planning.advanced: The worker reads engineering specifications to organize the exact step-by-step order across multiple cutting machines. For example, they review a part print to decide when to turn, drill, and mill a steel component for maximum efficiency.

workpiece-finishing.advanced: The worker chooses the best surface smoothing and cleaning techniques to meet exacting part specifications. For example, they choose bead blasting rather than hand filing to remove burrs from intricate plastic valves without scratching critical surfaces.

assembly-and-fitting.advanced: The worker creates custom holding jigs and positioning fixtures to help build intricate tooling components. For example, they build an angled holding fixture to grind steep chamfers onto delicate punch tips accurately and repeatedly.

blueprint-planning.advanced: The worker analyzes detailed blueprints to plan every cutting, grinding, and fitting step for custom tooling. For example, they map the construction sequence for a multi-piece metal stamping die from solid steel blocks.

machine-tool-operation.advanced: The worker configures and runs computer numerical control (CNC) machines to mill and grind parts to extremely precise finishes. For example, they program and operate a computerized milling machine to carve hardened steel die cavities.

material-shaping.basic: The worker cuts and trims raw metal pieces down to basic starting dimensions using manual tools. For example, they use a hacksaw and hand file to trim excess metal off a rectangular steel blank.

precision-measuring.advanced: The worker calculates minute dimensional allowances and visualizes how internal tool parts fit together in three dimensions. For example, they calculate clearance between punch and die openings to ensure stamped metal parts cut without tearing.

surface-finishing.advanced: The worker runs trial stampings on new tools and adjusts components until finished parts match exact requirements. For example, they stamp test parts in a press, inspect the edges, and adjust die spacing to fix burrs.
surface-finishing.basic: The worker uses hand files and abrasive sanding cloth to remove rough marks and smooth flat metal surfaces. For example, they rub a fine file and emery cloth over a steel block to polish away scratches.

finishing-and-cleaning.advanced: This involves melting and blowing away surplus metal from welded joints using an electrical torch. For example, a welder uses an electric arc gouging torch to carve away a bumpy, oversized seam on a steel frame.

metal-shaping.advanced: The worker disassembles damaged metal assemblies, straightens bent pieces, and welds them back together. For example, they unbolt a bent trailer frame, flatten the steel beam using a hydraulic press, and reweld the damaged joints.

quality-inspection.advanced: The worker detects hard-to-see weld imperfections and alerts supervisors when welding machines show signs of malfunction. For example, they spot microscopic surface cracks in a bead and report erratic voltage dips from the welding power supply.

safety-and-prep.advanced: The worker selects the appropriate welding process and heat settings based on metal composition and part angles. For example, they evaluate metal type and joint design to choose the correct wire, gas, and torch angle.
safety-and-prep.basic: The worker puts on protective gear and maintains safe workshop habits to avoid burns and fire hazards. For example, they wear a welding helmet and heavy leather gloves while checking that flammable materials are cleared away.

welding-techniques.advanced: The worker joins specialty metals while welding overhead without letting liquid metal drip or crack. For example, they weld a stainless steel joint located above their head on an industrial pipe rack using steady torch control.
welding-techniques.basic: The worker joins metal pieces resting flat on a bench using standard welding tools under guidance. For example, they guide a welding torch along a flat steel joint while a senior welder watches and gives tips.

workpiece-positioning.basic: The worker lines up metal pieces using rulers and squares, then clamps them tightly before welding begins. For example, they check a ninety-degree corner using an L-shaped square and clamp the steel bars to the welding table.

adjusting-machine-controls.advanced: This involves running sample pieces through automated welding machines and tweaking controls to achieve flawless seams. For example, an operator performs a test weld on scrap metal and adjusts electrical voltage to stop metal spatter.

checking-quality-and-records.advanced: This involves running tests on automated welding equipment to verify that completed joints meet strict manufacturing standards. For example, a technician inspects weld penetration using stress tests and logs machine output data to confirm quality requirements.

operating-welding-machines.advanced: This involves watching automated joining equipment closely to correct operational errors or halt machines when defects occur. For example, an operator notices a misaligned seam, presses the emergency stop, and adjusts wire feed speed before restarting.

preparing-metal-parts.advanced: This involves calculating exact dimensions and angles so metal pieces fit together flush before automated joining. For example, an operator calculates joint angles and trims steel tubing so edges align perfectly before entering a brazing furnace.

reading-production-specs.advanced: This involves reviewing factory timetables and instructing team members on preparing welding machines for upcoming jobs. For example, a senior operator checks daily production goals and tells coworkers which welding nozzles and wire spools to install.

setting-up-fixtures.advanced: This involves designing and assembling specialized clamps or frames to hold metal workpieces steady during welding. For example, a technician builds a metal frame that locks pipe joints in place for robotic welding.
setting-up-fixtures.basic: This involves checking reference tables to pick the right welding tips and filler metals with guidance. For example, a trainee looks at a chart to select the proper brass wire and torch nozzle.

adjusting-furnace-controls.advanced: This involves fixing temperature fluctuations in industrial ovens by adjusting gas and coolant valves. For example, an operator balances gas and air flow valves to keep an industrial furnace burner at a steady two thousand degrees.

cooling-treated-parts.advanced: This involves picking the right liquid bath to rapidly chill red-hot metals without cracking them. For example, an operator chooses an oil tank instead of water to cool delicate alloy blades without warping.

loading-furnace-stock.advanced: This involves managing the movement of massive raw metal blocks into industrial furnaces using cranes. For example, a furnace worker uses hand signals to guide a crane operator lowering a multi-ton steel block.

operating-heat-treat-machines.advanced: This involves preparing and running different industrial metal-hardening systems during production. For example, an operator sets electrical coils on an induction machine to harden shaft surfaces and later monitors flame burners hardening gear teeth.

reading-production-schedules.advanced: This involves reading multi-step heating and cooling instructions and updating furnace schedules for new products. For example, an operator schedules three distinct heating phases for a batch of high-strength steel gears.

recording-and-training.advanced: This involves instructing new staff on furnace operations and checking that they obey workshop safety practices. For example, an operator shows a new hire how to load parts safely and wear heat-resistant gloves around hot furnaces.

creating-layout-templates.advanced: This involves making full-scale physical patterns from sheet metal or wood to guide custom fabrication. For example, a worker constructs a curved wooden pattern to trace cutting outlines onto steel bridge girders.

fitting-structural-parts.advanced: This involves measuring, cutting, and assembling heavy metal sections that form the load-bearing framework of large structures. For example, a worker trims curved steel beams and joins them together to build a ship dividing wall.

marking-layout-lines.advanced: This involves drawing precise cut lines and welding symbols directly onto irregularly shaped metal pieces. For example, a worker scribes curved cutting boundaries and joint marks onto an uneven curved steel plate.

measuring-and-verifying.advanced: This involves checking pattern alignments and center marks on raw stock using delicate measuring tools. For example, a layout worker measures steel plate centerlines with precision calipers before cutting begins.

positioning-heavy-parts.advanced: This involves securing large metal plates inside ship structures using temporary supports before joining begins. For example, a worker positions steel hull sections and fastens metal braces to hold them steady for welding.

reading-technical-drawings.advanced: This involves clarifying missing measurements on engineering schematics and solving contradictory dimensions before fabrication starts. For example, a layout specialist notices overlapping part dimensions on an architectural blueprint and calculates corrected fabrication measurements.

coating-application.advanced: This involves controlling how long different items sit in chemical baths to produce an even finish. For example, a worker sets timers to submerge steel brackets for four minutes while leaving delicate plastic pieces in longer.

machine-setup.advanced: This involves diagnosing electrical or mechanical issues in coating equipment and fine-tuning controls. For example, an operator spots patchy finishes on metal parts, resets tank pump speeds, and adjusts chemical flow to fix the problem.

process-control.advanced: This involves regulating electrical power delivered to chemical baths so metal bonds at the correct depth. For example, an operator turns control dials to increase electrical voltage until protective chrome coats steel bolts to exact specifications.

production-records.advanced: This involves reviewing daily logs and output data to find patterns and speed up manufacturing. For example, an operator compares daily tank temperature charts with defect rates to determine which settings minimize wasted chemical solutions.

quality-inspection.advanced: This involves establishing guidelines for finished coatings and teaching coworkers how to spot minor flaws. For example, a worker creates a visual checklist and coaches colleagues to identify faint bubbles or uneven gloss under bright inspection lights.

surface-preparation.advanced: This involves choosing and applying specialized cleaning solutions to strip heavy dirt from detailed components before coating. For example, a worker soaks grooved brass valves in heated chemical baths to dissolve grease hidden in tight crevices.

machine-maintenance.advanced: This involves figuring out why sharpening machinery is malfunctioning and installing replacement components. For example, a worker identifies a worn spindle bearing causing grinding wheel vibration, disassembles the housing, and bolts in a fresh replacement part.

machine-setup.advanced: This involves interpreting technical diagrams to arrange sharpening machines and choose the right grinding sequence. For example, a worker studies a drill bit drawing, clamps specialized holding fixtures, and installs the required abrasive wheels in order.

operational-monitoring.advanced: This involves watching and listening to running equipment to detect warning signs before breakdowns occur. For example, an operator notices a faint hum and rising motor heat, stopping the grinder to lubricate dry gears before damage occurs.

precision-adjustments.advanced: This involves calculating sharp blade angles and tilting machine tables to achieve exact cutting edges. For example, a worker calculates the clearance angle for an industrial saw tooth and pivots the grinding head by three degrees.

quality-inspection.advanced: This involves creating measurement guidelines for sharpened blades and teaching coworkers how to verify them. For example, a worker writes acceptable sharpness guidelines and demonstrates how to check cutting tool edges using a magnifying glass gauge.

surface-finishing.advanced: This involves grinding and polishing detailed metal surfaces to strict dimensional standards without assistance. For example, a worker guides a fine abrasive wheel across the curved teeth of a custom metal gear until all rough edges vanish.

color-and-text-proofing.advanced: This involves using light-measuring instruments to check ink darkness and color transitions across printed sheets. For example, a technician presses an electronic optical meter against a test sheet to confirm cyan ink thickness matches target darkness values.

digital-file-preparation.advanced: This involves configuring scanner hardware to capture images with exact color tone depth and grid lines. For example, a technician configures scanner software settings to digitize an oil painting with high dot density for sharp poster reproduction.
digital-file-preparation.basic: This involves typing job specifications into prepress computer systems and organizing electronic design files. For example, a worker enters client page dimensions into a database and saves incoming artwork files into designated press folders.

equipment-care-and-layout.basic: This involves cleaning lenses, rollers, and machinery while following instructions from experienced colleagues. For example, a worker wipes down scanner glass with lint-free cloths and adjusts paper tray guides under a supervisor's step-by-step guidance.

image-quality-checks.advanced: This involves looking through a microscope to confirm printing plates have correctly sized ink dots. For example, a technician inspects an aluminum printing plate under magnification to verify tiny halftone dots match required size measurements.

plate-making-operation.advanced: This involves choosing printing plate materials depending on how many copies need to be printed. For example, a technician selects heavy-duty metal plates for a hundred-thousand-copy magazine run instead of thinner plastic plates for short jobs.

proof-printing-and-scaling.advanced: This involves creating accurate sample prints using computer software and calibrated printers to preview finished jobs. For example, a technician outputs a color-matched sample page of a magazine cover so editors can review appearance before mass printing.
proof-printing-and-scaling.basic: This involves using a circular handheld calculator wheel to figure out percentage reductions for pictures or text. For example, a worker lines up original and desired photo dimensions on the wheel to calculate the reduction percentage.

ink-and-material-prep.advanced: This involves blending base inks to match exact color shades and checking paper quality for demanding jobs. For example, an operator measures pigments on a precision scale to mix custom corporate blue ink for glossy brochures.
ink-and-material-prep.basic: This involves pouring ink into press reservoirs and inspecting paper supply under supervision. For example, a worker scoops ink into machine wells and checks paper stacks for moisture or bent edges while an experienced operator watches.

job-planning-and-records.advanced: This involves evaluating upcoming print orders to arrange efficient daily production runs and manage supplies. For example, an operator schedules projects using identical paper stock back-to-back to minimize machine adjustments and track paper inventory.
job-planning-and-records.basic: This involves reading production paperwork and typing machine parameters into control panels with help. For example, a worker checks a job ticket for print quantities and enters paper dimensions into the machine console under supervisor direction.

press-maintenance-and-cleaning.advanced: This involves fixing minor mechanical faults and planning regular service timetables for printing equipment. For example, an operator replaces worn paper feeder belts and creates a weekly schedule for cleaning and lubricating cylinder bearings.
press-maintenance-and-cleaning.basic: This involves washing ink reservoirs and printing surfaces by following written guidelines. For example, a worker follows a checklist to scrape leftover ink from metal trays and wipe down printing plates using solvent rags at shift end.

press-monitoring-and-control.advanced: This involves adjusting room humidity, temperature, and machine ink feeds to keep print quality consistent. For example, an operator regulates room moisture controls and lowers ink roller speeds to stop paper pages from smearing.
press-monitoring-and-control.basic: This involves watching machine warning lights and tweaking ink supply keys with coworker guidance. For example, a helper spots a low-ink screen warning and turns ink fountain screws to increase flow while an experienced printer assists.

press-setup-and-loading.advanced: This involves resolving cylinder misalignments so different ink colors line up seamlessly on printed pages. For example, an operator spots blue ink printing slightly off-center and turns cylinder adjustment dials until color layers overlap perfectly.
press-setup-and-loading.basic: This involves stacking paper into machine feeders and mounting printing plates while following senior direction. For example, an assistant loads paper reams into the feeder tray and tightens plate clamps on the cylinder under supervisor oversight.

quality-inspection-and-proofs.advanced: This involves establishing print quality benchmarks and training colleagues to spot subtle defects. For example, an operator sets acceptable color-drift limits and coaches team members on using magnifying lenses to spot fine ink streaks on finished covers.
quality-inspection-and-proofs.basic: This involves taking sample sheets from running presses and reviewing alignment alongside a supervisor. For example, an assistant pulls a printed sheet from the delivery tray and compares alignment marks against a master copy with supervisor assistance.

binding-operations.advanced: This involves running heavy-duty folding and pressing equipment during large-scale manufacturing runs. For example, an operator feeds printed sheets through automated folding machines and uses hydraulic presses to flatten thousands of book sections before spine gluing.
binding-operations.basic: This involves fastening folded sheets and cover linings together using basic shop machinery and adhesives. For example, a worker applies glue along folded page packets and presses protective endpapers against book spines using a hand press.

machine-maintenance.advanced: This involves identifying causes of equipment breakdowns and completing quick mechanical repairs during production. For example, an operator traces a conveyor jam to a broken rubber drive belt, replaces the belt, and restarts the book assembly line.
machine-maintenance.basic: This involves clearing debris from bindery equipment and oiling moving mechanisms according to clear instructions. For example, a worker brushes paper dust away from trimmer blades and squirts oil into conveyor bearings as directed by the supervisor.

machine-setup.advanced: This involves configuring cutting blades and pressure rollers to handle different publication formats. For example, an operator repositions trimmer knives and adjusts roller spacing on a binding machine when switching from small pocket novels to large hardcover textbooks.
machine-setup.basic: This involves adding adhesive to machine tanks and adjusting valve controls for proper glue application. For example, a worker pours glue into a binder reservoir and turns a dial to regulate adhesive flow for paperback books.

order-records.advanced: This involves reading detailed job sheets to set up equipment efficiently and keep work moving smoothly. For example, a worker reads order specifications for hardcover novel binding, arranging machine stations so trimming and foil stamping run without delays.

quality-inspection.advanced: This involves inspecting finished publications for small flaws and finding ways to prevent future assembly problems. For example, an inspector notices loose pages in sample catalogs and recommends tightening clamp pressure on the binder conveyor.

shipping-training.advanced: This involves teaching new employees safe handling and configuration procedures for automated finishing equipment. For example, an experienced operator demonstrates how to adjust protective blade guards and load paper safely into an automatic folding machine.

chemical-mixing.advanced: This involves calculating and blending exact proportions of dyes and bleaching agents to match fabric colors. For example, a worker mixes blue dye powder and water to restore the original navy shade of a faded jacket.

loading-flow-control.advanced: This involves detecting uneven liquid flow while loading tankers and tuning pump speeds to prevent bottlenecks. For example, a loader notices liquid foaming inside a rail tanker and lowers pump pressure to maintain steady filling.

loading-process-monitoring.advanced: This involves collaborating with multiple teams to fix flow stoppages and keep materials moving. For example, a loader coordinates with pipeline workers and ship crews to clear a clogged valve and resume oil pumping.

material-handling-equipment.advanced: This involves handling specialized mechanical gear to transfer liquids into or out of train cars safely. For example, an operator connects a heavy articulated unloading arm to a train car hatch and opens discharge valves.

operational-data-recording.advanced: This involves reviewing shipping logs for errors and teaching newer staff proper recordkeeping methods. For example, a loader verifies liquid volume figures against scale weight tickets and demonstrates correct data entry steps to a trainee.

vessel-positioning-and-sealing.advanced: This involves positioning transport containers accurately and verifying all closures are airtight. For example, a loader checks tank car placement on the tracks and tests hatch seals to prevent vapor leaks before departure.
